doc.title: James Chirillo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Does composing affect improvising; keeping standards fresh
summary: Great composers can play, a Beethoven anecdote, and the challenge of making a familiar tune sound fresh.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Does your — do you think being a composer and having studied composing affects the way you improvise?

Of course. Yeah. Most really great composers could play something, and usually pretty darn good. Beethoven you know, when he played his first piano concerto, I forget for what prince he was writing it for but whatever, but he showed up and the piano was tuned, the piano concerto was written in C, but the piano was tuned and it had settled like a half step low. So he played his part in D flat that day.

So I guess the point is yeah, when you’re writing something the challenge is, especially if it’s like how most jazz players — let me back up a bit. If you’re playing a standard tune, a tune that the audience already knows, that your listening audience already is familiar with, be it by Irvin Berlin or who knows, but they already know the melody. Now you’re going to do it in a way that, the challenge is, hopefully, that it’s going to sound fresh to them. So and that doesn’t mean like totally rewrite the tune. Maybe you want to throw in a little different harmony or something, okay. But then even when you’re playing, if you’ve got that same old tune and you’re with a group or whatever, maybe you have one horn or maybe it’s just guitar trio or whatever. How many choruses of that are you going play where it’s going to be exactly the same? You’re not going to change key on every chorus. You’re not going to totally rewrite the harmony on every chorus.
